title: Global and fine-grained magnitude pruning reduce on-disk model size and maintain or improve accuracy after fine-tuning
content: Both global unstructured magnitude pruning, which applies a uniform sparsity ratio across all weights, and fine-grained layer-wise magnitude pruning, which applies per-layer magnitude thresholds, substantially reduce on-disk model size when the model state is stored sparsely by keeping only nonzero weight values and their positions. Empirically, pruned models achieve size reductions of approximately 4–9× at high sparsity (80–90%), depending on dataset and method; for instance, global pruning on the Cora node classification task achieves a baseline-to-pruned size ratio of 4.76× at 80% sparsity and 8.98× at 90% sparsity. Accuracy after pruning often remains near baseline or improves following fine-tuning; for example, global pruning on the Cora node classification setup shows accuracy recovering from values near 0.86 to 0.90 ± 0.01 after fine-tuning at certain pruning levels. These effects were observed across the evaluated GNN architectures (SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, GIN) and datasets (Cora, Proteins, BBBP).

title: Global pruning is more stable across tasks, while fine-grained pruning is higher-risk/higher-reward and preferable for structurally sensitive tasks
content: In the comparison of the two magnitude-based pruning methods applied to the GNN architectures (SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, GIN) and tasks (node classification on Cora, link prediction on Cora, graph classification on BBBP and Proteins), global unstructured pruning exhibits more consistent behavior across tasks: it tolerates moderate sparsity (30–60%) with small accuracy degradation, and does not require per-layer tuning. Fine-grained layer-wise pruning yields larger accuracy drops when applied without fine-tuning (e.g., on Cora node classification, accuracy drops from 0.86 at baseline to 0.76 at 90% sparsity without fine-tuning), but when followed by fine-tuning, it can recover or surpass baseline accuracy on structurally sensitive tasks such as node classification on Cora (accuracy recovers to approximately 0.89 at 90% sparsity after fine-tuning). On other tasks, such as graph classification on BBBP and Proteins, fine-grained pruning with fine-tuning does not recover baseline accuracy at high sparsity. Overall, global pruning is lower-variance and safer for general compression, while fine-grained pruning is higher-variance but may preserve critical substructures and yield better accuracy recovery on some datasets.

title: Early convolutional layers tolerate more pruning, while linear/classifier layers are more sensitive
content: Layer-wise analysis of sparsity under global unstructured magnitude pruning applied to the GNN architectures (GNNNet on BBBP, SplineConv on Cora node classification, HGP-SL on Proteins) reveals heterogeneous sensitivity: early convolutional layers (e.g., the first GCNConv layer in GNNNet, the spline convolution layers in SplineConv, and the linear transform layer before message passing in HGP-SL) maintain a low proportion of zero weights even at high global sparsity targets, indicating tolerance to pruning. In contrast, linear projection layers and final classifier MLPs (e.g., the MLP layer in GNNNet, the linear projection layers in SplineConv, and the classifier MLP layers in HGP-SL) exhibit a high proportion of zero weights even at low global sparsity, indicating greater sensitivity to pruning. This pattern motivates dynamic, layer-specific pruning thresholds rather than a uniform sparsity target.

title: Pruning does not reliably reduce inference latency or memory usage; resource metrics are non-monotonic and dataset-dependent
content: In the experiments on GNN architectures (SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, GIN) and datasets (Cora node classification, Cora link prediction, BBBP, Proteins), reductions in parameter count from pruning did not translate into consistent decreases in inference time or memory usage. Inference latency remained largely unchanged across sparsity levels. Memory usage and CPU/energy consumption showed non-monotonic, dataset- and sparsity-dependent patterns: for global pruning, CPU usage peaks at 70% sparsity across datasets; for fine-grained pruning, CPU and energy consumption exhibit sharp spikes and bimodal profiles, with energy consumption being higher than global pruning at low-to-moderate sparsities (0.1–0.3), while global pruning is more energy-efficient at medium-to-high sparsities (0.4–0.8).

title: Sparse state compression with shape and nonzero values reduces on-disk size at high sparsity
content: A practical sparse-state storage method writes for each parameter tensor either the full tensor when it is entirely zero, or a sparse record containing the tensor shape and the array of nonzero values together with an implicit binary mask derived from nonzero positions. This materially reduces on-disk model sizes for pruned GNNs with architectures SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, and GIN. This approach yields meaningful disk savings only beyond high sparsity levels (empirically, significant reductions appear when sparsity exceeds roughly 80%), because storing sparse indices and metadata offsets incurs overhead at lower sparsities.

title: DQ-INT8 and QAT-INT8 recover accuracy with lower energy and CPU; INT4 variants trade accuracy for efficiency
content: Evaluating quantization schemes on the GIN graph-classification model reveals that Degree-Quant (DQ) with INT8 and Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) with INT8 consistently recover most or all accuracy lost to reduced precision and often improve resource metrics. For the BBBP dataset, DQ-INT8 achieves accuracy 0.83 ± 0.01, inference time 2.04 s, and energy 24.78 ± 0.17 J; QAT-INT8 achieves similar accuracy (0.83 ± 0.01) and inference time (2.04 s) but higher energy (32.45 ± 2.98 J). For the Proteins dataset, DQ-INT8 achieves accuracy 0.72 ± 0.01 and energy 28.74 ± 2.72 J; QAT-INT8 achieves accuracy 0.72 ± 0.01 and energy 37.19 ± 3.09 J. INT4 variants (QAT-INT4, DQ-INT4) are less stable: they can be faster in training duration but often incur larger accuracy drops (e.g., DQ-INT4 on BBBP: accuracy 0.77 ± 0.02, energy 33.69 ± 4.18 J; on Proteins: accuracy 0.61 ± 0.02, energy 30.26 ± 3.39 J). These results hold across the BBBP and Proteins datasets.

title: A^{2}Q shows high memory overhead and inconsistent accuracy
content: The aggregation-aware mixed-precision method A^{2}Q demonstrates dataset-dependent behavior and unusually large memory footprints in quantization experiments on the GIN model with the BBBP and Proteins datasets. On BBBP, A^{2}Q achieves accuracy 0.59 ± 0.01 and consumes 80.15 ± 0.49 GB of memory; on Proteins, it achieves accuracy 0.70 ± 0.00 and consumes 77.35 ± 0.78 GB of memory. In comparison, QAT-INT8 and DQ-INT8 use approximately 37–47 GB of memory and achieve higher accuracy (e.g., 0.83 ± 0.01 on BBBP, 0.72 ± 0.01 on Proteins). A^{2}Q is also the slowest in training duration (e.g., 159.6 s on BBBP). This makes A^{2}Q an inconsistent choice for resource-limited deployments.

title: Lottery ticket hypothesis does not hold for the evaluated GNNs under tested pruning regimes
content: The lottery ticket hypothesis (LTH) posits that a randomly initialized neural network contains a subnetwork that, when trained in isolation, can match the test accuracy of the original network. In experiments applying the evaluated pruning and fine-tuning workflows to the GNN architectures (SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, GIN) and datasets (Cora, Proteins, BBBP), no such subnetwork was found: smaller subnetworks obtained by the evaluated pruning schedules generally failed to match full-model accuracy without careful task- and layer-specific tuning. This indicates that the LTH, as tested here, is not supported for these graph models and tasks.

title: L2 regularization: moderate rates preserve accuracy, aggressive rates degrade accuracy and cause resource spikes
content: Systematic sweeps of L2 regularization coefficients across four datasets (BBBP, Cora node classification, Cora link prediction, Proteins) with the respective GNN models show that modest regularization (rates below approximately 1×10^{-2}) preserves accuracy; for example, on BBBP accuracy remains 0.84–0.85 for rates up to 10^{-3}, on Cora node classification accuracy is 0.87–0.90 for rates up to 10^{-2}, on Proteins accuracy is 0.82 for rates up to 10^{-2}, and on Cora link prediction accuracy declines gradually from 0.95 to 0.92 for rates up to 10^{-2}. Aggressive regularization rates (≥ 0.1) cause sharp accuracy degradation across datasets and may produce spikes in energy and CPU usage at intermediate values (e.g., on BBBP, energy reaches 80 J and CPU reaches 58% at rates 0.6–0.8; on Cora link prediction, energy spikes to 77 J at rates 10^{2}–10^{6}). Very large regularization (e.g., 10^{2}–10^{6}) sometimes reduces resource consumption but at the cost of greatly reduced accuracy (e.g., on Cora node classification, accuracy drops to 0.14–0.28 at rates ≥ 0.1).
